# Diagnosing Bent Intake Push Rods on Small Engines

When a push rod bends, it is almost never an isolated mechanical failure. It is usually the symptom of a larger issue that allowed excessive force to transfer from the valve train down into the rocker arms and lifters. In your specific case involving a Briggs & Stratton 18.5HP Intek motor (Model 31P777-0602-B2), the evidence points strongly toward hydraulic lock caused by liquid fuel in the combustion chamber or oil gallery, rather than simple wear.

The most telling clue is the presence of gas in the engine oil and the strong smell of gasoline immediately after failure. On a two-stroke cycle or an overhead valve four-stroke like the Intek, this indicates a breach between the crankcase or carburetor bowl and the cylinder head. If you suspect the float was gunked up initially, cleaning the carburetor only fixes the *current* state; it does not explain how the liquid got there in the first place if the float needle valve is functional. However, if the float assembly failed previously, allowing fuel to flood the crankcase, that fluid can migrate past piston rings into the cylinder.

If you have a functioning head gasket and intact piston rings, liquid cannot enter the cylinder during compression stroke unless it was introduced directly through the intake port while the engine was running. This leads to **hydrostatic lock**. When a valve is closed and fuel floods the cylinder, the next firing attempt forces that incompressible fluid against the piston. Since steel pistons cannot compress gasoline, the force transfers upward, bending the push rod or cracking the head.

You noted the intake valve sticks slightly. While minor sticking is common due to carbon buildup on these older Intek models, significant binding can be catastrophic under high load. When the engine hits full throttle, cylinder pressure spikes dramatically. If the intake valve cannot open fully or opens late due to sticky guides or deposits, compression builds up behind the closed valve. This trapped pressure acts like a hydraulic brake on the camshaft and push rod system. While a few taps might free it during manual inspection, dynamic operation at high RPM generates enough force to snap the rod if the clearance is even marginally tight.

Regarding your question about moving valve guides: on Briggs Intek engines, the intake guide is often loose enough that it can be tapped out with a plastic hammer or a specific tool without removing the head. A "good" guide should slide in and out of its housing freely but not rattle excessively when the engine is off. If the guide has migrated downward (a common failure mode on these engines), it reduces the effective length of the valve stem, altering the lash settings. When you adjust the rocker arm clearance based on a shortened stem, the valve opens too late or hits the push rod early in the cycle, causing binding and eventual bending.

Before replacing the rod, verify the guide position. Remove the intake valve from the head. If it slides out easily with minimal effort compared to the exhaust valve (which you noted moves freely), the guide is likely worn or displaced. Check the depth of the guide in the head; if it sits proud or recessed significantly beyond factory specs, the entire cylinder head assembly needs attention, not just a rod replacement.

If the guides are within spec and the gasket shows no external weeping or internal coolant mixing (if applicable), replace the intake valve with an aftermarket stainless steel unit if available. Stock valves on these engines often suffer from thermal expansion issues that contribute to sticking. Finally, ensure your carburetor float height is set precisely according to the manual; even a 1/32-inch error can cause flooding in high-humidity conditions, setting the stage for hydrostatic lock.

If you proceed with installing a new rod, recheck the rocker arm clearance after the engine has cooled and warmed up once more. Push rods on this platform expand slightly when hot, so initial cold-set clearances must account for thermal growth to prevent immediate post-start failure.
